subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Pressure as perpendicular force per unit area
Count particles with the amount of substance
The ideal gas as a model of real gases
From the three gas laws to PV/T = constant
The ideal gas law in two forms
Pressure from molecular collisions and P = ⅓ρv²
Internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas
When a real gas behaves like an ideal gas

questions.q: A student pushes on a horizontal table top through a flat pad of area 8.0 cm². The force exerted by the pad on the table is 40 N, directed at 30° to the vertical. What pressure does the pad exert on the table?
optionWhy: A student who divides the whole 40 N by the area gets 5.0 × 10⁴ Pa. The horizontal component of the force pushes along the table and produces no pressure; only the perpendicular component, 40 cos 30° = 34.6 N, counts.
Only the component perpendicular to the table produces pressure. The vertical component is 40 cos 30° = 34.6 N, and A = 8.0 cm² = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², so P = 34.6 ÷ 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 4.3 × 10⁴ Pa.

A student who uses 40 sin 30° = 20 N has taken the component parallel to the table. The angle is measured from the vertical, so the component perpendicular to the table is the adjacent one, 40 cos 30° = 34.6 N.
A student who converts 8.0 cm² to 8.0 × 10⁻² m² has divided by 100, the factor for lengths. For an area the factor is squared: 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², so A = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² and P is 100 times larger.
questions.explain: Only the component perpendicular to the table produces pressure. The vertical component is 40 cos 30° = 34.6 N, and A = 8.0 cm² = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², so P = 34.6 ÷ 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 4.3 × 10⁴ Pa.
questions.working: Perpendicular component of the force: F⊥ = 40 N × cos 30° = 34.6 N. Area: A = 8.0 cm² = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². P = F⊥/A = 34.6 N ÷ 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 4.33 × 10⁴ Pa ≈ 4.3 × 10⁴ Pa.

questions.q: Two sealed flasks each contain 0.50 mol of gas. Flask X holds helium, a monatomic gas of molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹. Flask Y holds nitrogen, which consists of N₂ molecules; the molar mass of nitrogen atoms is 14 g mol⁻¹. Which statement correctly compares the two samples?
options: The number of N atoms equals the number of He atoms, and the nitrogen has 3.5 times the mass.
The number of N₂ molecules equals the number of He atoms, and the nitrogen has seven times the mass.
The two samples have equal masses, because each flask holds the same amount of substance.
The nitrogen has more molecules than the helium has atoms, since a mole of heavier particles holds more.
optionWhy: A student who takes the molar mass of nitrogen gas to be that of its atoms, 14 g mol⁻¹, gets a mass of 7.0 g and a ratio of 3.5. Nitrogen gas is made of N₂ molecules of molar mass 28 g mol⁻¹, so the sample has a mass of 14 g, and it contains twice as many atoms as the helium flask, not the same number.

The amount of substance is a count of particles, N = nN_A, so equal amounts contain equal numbers of particles: 0.50 mol of N₂ molecules and 0.50 mol of He atoms. The masses differ because the molar masses differ: 0.50 × 28 = 14 g of nitrogen against 0.50 × 4.0 = 2.0 g of helium, a ratio of 7.

A student who identifies the amount of substance with mass picks this. Amount of substance is a count of particles in moles; the mass of a sample is nM, so equal amounts of substances with different molar masses have different masses: 2.0 g of helium and 14 g of nitrogen here.

A student who thinks the number of particles in a mole depends on the substance picks this. One mole of anything contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles, so 0.50 mol of nitrogen contains exactly as many molecules as 0.50 mol of helium contains atoms. The heavier molecules make the sample heavier, not more numerous.
questions.explain: The amount of substance is a count of particles, N = nN_A, so equal amounts contain equal numbers of particles: 0.50 mol of N₂ molecules and 0.50 mol of He atoms. The masses differ because the molar masses differ: 0.50 × 28 = 14 g of nitrogen against 0.50 × 4.0 = 2.0 g of helium, a ratio of 7.
questions.working:
The amount of substance counts particles: N = nN_A, so 0.50 mol of He atoms and 0.50 mol of N₂ molecules contain the same number of particles, 0.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.0 × 10²³ each.
Mass of helium = nM = 0.50 mol × 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 g.
Molar mass of N₂ = 2 × 14 = 28 g mol⁻¹, so mass of nitrogen = 0.50 mol × 28 g mol⁻¹ = 14 g.
Ratio of masses = 14/2.0 = 7.0, so the nitrogen has seven times the mass of the helium.

questions.q: At room temperature and atmospheric pressure, measurements on helium agree closely with PV = nRT. A student concludes: 'Helium is an ideal gas.' Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?
options: Justified: helium is monatomic and unreactive, and this makes it one of the ideal gases.
Not justified: helium atoms collide with one another, but ideal gas molecules do not collide.
Justified: agreement with PV = nRT shows that every assumption of the model is exactly true for helium.
Not justified: helium is a real gas that the model approximates closely under these conditions.
optionWhy: A student who thinks some gases simply are ideal picks this. No real gas is ideal; helium can be liquefied, which is impossible for an ideal gas. 'Ideal' describes a model that helium approximates well under some conditions.

A student who reads 'no intermolecular forces' as 'no collisions' picks this. Ideal gas molecules do collide, elastically and briefly; the model excludes forces between molecules only while they are apart.

A student who thinks a model that predicts well must be literally true picks this. The model's assumptions (point particles, no forces between collisions) are never exactly true; agreement shows only that the simplifications have negligible effect under these conditions.

The ideal gas is a model. Helium atoms have a small volume and exert weak attractions, so helium is a real gas; under these conditions the effects are tiny and the model fits well. At high pressure or near 4 K, where helium liquefies, it deviates.
questions.explain: The ideal gas is a model. Helium atoms have a small volume and exert weak attractions, so helium is a real gas; under these conditions the effects are tiny and the model fits well. At high pressure or near 4 K, where helium liquefies, it deviates.

questions.q: Air in a sealed syringe has a volume of 60 cm³ at a pressure of 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 17 °C. The plunger is pushed in quickly until the volume is 20 cm³, and the air warms to 47 °C. Treat the air as an ideal gas. What is its new pressure?
optionWhy: A student who applies Boyle's law, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, gets 3.00 × 10⁵ Pa. Boyle's law needs constant temperature; here the air warms from 290 K to 320 K, so the pressure rises by a further factor of 320/290.
Using P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ with T in kelvin: P₂ = 1.00 × 10⁵ × (60/20) × (320/290) = 3.31 × 10⁵ Pa. Both the compression and the warming raise the pressure.
A student who uses the Celsius temperatures multiplies by 47/17 = 2.76. The gas laws need absolute temperatures: 17 °C = 290 K and 47 °C = 320 K, a ratio of only 1.10.

A student who multiplies the pressure by 'new over old' for each variable uses 20/60 for the volume and gets a pressure LOWER than at the start. Compression raises the pressure: P ∝ 1/V, so the volume ratio must be 60/20.
questions.explain: Using P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ with T in kelvin: P₂ = 1.00 × 10⁵ × (60/20) × (320/290) = 3.31 × 10⁵ Pa. Both the compression and the warming raise the pressure.
questions.working: T₁ = 17 + 273 = 290 K; T₂ = 47 + 273 = 320 K. P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ gives P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa × (60 cm³/20 cm³) × (320 K/290 K) = 3.31 × 10⁵ Pa. (The volume units cancel in the ratio, so cm³ may be used.)

questions.q: On a pressure–volume diagram (pressure on the vertical axis, volume on the horizontal axis), a fixed mass of ideal gas moves from state X to state Y along a horizontal straight line. At X the volume is 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ and the temperature is 27 °C; at Y the volume is 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³. What is the temperature at Y, and under what condition does the change X → Y take place?
options: 327 °C, at constant pressure
54 °C, at constant pressure
27 °C, at constant temperature
−123 °C, at constant pressure
optionWhy: A horizontal line on a P–V diagram means the pressure is constant, so V/T is constant with T in kelvin. The volume doubles, so T doubles from 300 K to 600 K, which is 327 °C.
A student who doubles the Celsius temperature gets 54 °C. V ∝ T only for absolute temperature: 27 °C = 300 K doubles to 600 K, which is 327 °C.

A student who reads a horizontal line as 'no change' takes the change to be at constant temperature. Along a horizontal line on a P–V diagram the pressure is fixed; constant-temperature changes lie on curves on which PV is constant.

A student who treats volume and temperature as inversely related, like pressure and volume, halves the kelvin temperature to 150 K = −123 °C. At constant pressure a gas expands when heated: V/T is constant, so doubling V doubles T.
questions.explain: A horizontal line on a P–V diagram means the pressure is constant, so V/T is constant with T in kelvin. The volume doubles, so T doubles from 300 K to 600 K, which is 327 °C.
questions.working: Horizontal line on a P–V diagram: P constant. V/T = constant with T in K: T_X = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T_Y = T_X × (V_Y/V_X) = 300 K × (6.0 × 10⁻³/3.0 × 10⁻³) = 600 K = 327 °C.

questions.q: Two identical rigid containers are at the same temperature and the same pressure. One holds hydrogen (H₂) and the other holds carbon dioxide (CO₂). Both gases behave as ideal gases. How do the numbers of molecules in the two containers compare?
options: They are equal, as equal pressure, volume and temperature mean equal numbers.
There are more H₂ molecules, as smaller molecules leave room for more of them.
There are more CO₂ molecules, as the heavier gas is the larger amount of substance.
There are fewer CO₂ molecules, as each heavier molecule strikes the walls harder.
optionWhy: PV = Nk_B T contains no property of the molecules, so equal P, V and T mean equal N. A CO₂ molecule is heavier, but at the same temperature it moves more slowly, and the two effects on pressure cancel.

A student who pictures the molecules filling the container picks this. In a gas the molecules occupy a negligible fraction of the volume, so their size does not limit how many fit; N depends only on P, V and T.

A student who treats the amount of substance as a mass picks this. The amount of substance counts molecules; from PV = nRT, equal P, V and T give equal n and so equal numbers of molecules, whatever their mass.

A student who forgets that heavier molecules move more slowly at the same temperature picks this. Each CO₂ molecule does transfer more momentum per collision, but it collides less often; at the same T the average pressure contribution per molecule is the same.
questions.explain: PV = Nk_B T contains no property of the molecules, so equal P, V and T mean equal N. A CO₂ molecule is heavier, but at the same temperature it moves more slowly, and the two effects on pressure cancel.

questions.q: A sample of helium at 300 K has a density of 0.160 kg m⁻³. The mean speed of its atoms is 1.26 × 10³ m s⁻¹, and the mean of the squares of their speeds is 1.87 × 10⁶ m² s⁻². Treat helium as an ideal gas. What is its pressure?
optionWhy: A student who squares the mean speed uses (1.26 × 10³)² = 1.59 × 10⁶ m² s⁻². The equation needs the mean of the squares, which is larger than the square of the mean because fast atoms count for more when speeds are squared first.

A student who leaves out the ⅓ gets a pressure three times too large. The atoms move randomly in three dimensions, so on average only a third of v² comes from the velocity component perpendicular to any one wall.
A student who writes P = ½ρv² has borrowed the ½ from E_k = ½mv². The ⅓ in the pressure equation has a different origin: averaging random motion over three dimensions.
In P = ⅓ρv², v² is the mean of the squared speeds, 1.87 × 10⁶ m² s⁻². P = ⅓ × 0.160 × 1.87 × 10⁶ = 9.97 × 10⁴ Pa.
questions.explain: In P = ⅓ρv², v² is the mean of the squared speeds, 1.87 × 10⁶ m² s⁻². P = ⅓ × 0.160 × 1.87 × 10⁶ = 9.97 × 10⁴ Pa.
questions.working: P = ⅓ρv², with v² the mean of the squared speeds: P = ⅓ × 0.160 kg m⁻³ × 1.87 × 10⁶ m² s⁻² = 9.97 × 10⁴ Pa. The mean speed, 1.26 × 10³ m s⁻¹, is not needed.

questions.q: A fixed mass of ideal monatomic gas is compressed slowly to half its volume while its temperature is kept constant. What happens to the internal energy U of the gas?
options: It increases, as the closer molecules store more intermolecular potential energy.
It does not change, as the temperature and so the mean kinetic energy are fixed.
It increases, because work is done on the gas while it is being compressed.
It doubles, because the pressure doubles and molecules hit the walls twice as often.
optionWhy: A student who pictures compression like squeezing a spring picks this. An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces and therefore no intermolecular potential energy, whatever the separation of its molecules.

For an ideal monatomic gas the internal energy is only the translational kinetic energy of the molecules, U = (3/2)Nk_B T. With N and T fixed, U is unchanged; the work done on the gas is transferred out of it thermally.

A student who thinks work done on a gas must raise its internal energy picks this. In a slow compression at constant temperature, an equal amount of energy leaves the gas thermally, so U does not change.

A student who links internal energy to pressure picks this. The pressure does double, because collisions with the walls become twice as frequent, but the molecules' speeds and kinetic energies are unchanged, so U is unchanged.
questions.explain: For an ideal monatomic gas the internal energy is only the translational kinetic energy of the molecules, U = (3/2)Nk_B T. With N and T fixed, U is unchanged; the work done on the gas is transferred out of it thermally.
questions.working: For an ideal monatomic gas U = (3/2)Nk_B T. N is fixed (fixed mass) and T is constant, so ΔU = (3/2)Nk_B ΔT = 0.

questions.q: A real gas at a temperature a little above its boiling point is compressed to a high density. Its measured pressure is found to be lower than the value that PV = nRT predicts for the same n, V and T. Which is the best explanation?
options: The molecules take up part of the volume, which leaves less space for the gas and so lowers its pressure.
Collisions between real molecules are inelastic, so the molecules slow down and the pressure falls.
Attractive forces between the molecules pull those near a wall back, so they strike it with less momentum.
Near the boiling point the molecules have almost stopped moving, so few of them reach the walls.
optionWhy: A student who reasons that less space means less gas picks this. The volume of the molecules reduces the free space they move in, so they strike the walls MORE often; on its own this raises the pressure above the ideal value.

A student who thinks molecular collisions lose energy picks this. If they did, a sealed gas would cool and its pressure fall with nothing leaving it, which is not observed; the deviation is caused by attractive forces, not by energy loss.

Close to the boiling point and at high density, intermolecular attractions are significant. A molecule approaching a wall is pulled back towards the bulk of the gas, so it delivers less momentum to the wall, and the pressure is below the ideal value.

A student who links 'cold' with 'stationary' picks this. The molecules still move at hundreds of metres per second near the boiling point. The deviation arises because attractions become significant compared with their kinetic energy.
questions.explain: Close to the boiling point and at high density, intermolecular attractions are significant. A molecule approaching a wall is pulled back towards the bulk of the gas, so it delivers less momentum to the wall, and the pressure is below the ideal value.
